title: Channel Letter Signs in Alpharetta, GA: Permit Rules, Timeline, and How to Order Factory-Direct
excerpt: Ordering channel letter signs for an Alpharetta, GA business? See the city's permit rules, the 45-business-day review limit, UL 48 requirements, and factory-direct ordering.

runs.text: Picture the owner of a new dental office in an Alpharetta business park. She has two local quotes for illuminated channel letters, and both are higher than she expected. A friend mentions that some manufacturers sell directly. That sounds appealing, until she asks the next questions. Does the city require a permit? Who installs a sign that ships from a factory? What happens at inspection?

Those are the right questions, and they are worth answering before any sign is ordered. This guide covers how sign permits work in Alpharetta, what the city says about timelines and electrical work, and how ordering channel letters factory-direct fits into that process.

One point up front. BASISSIGN is a manufacturer, not a local installation company, and we do not have a shop in Alpharetta. We build the sign and ship it with a mounting template and wiring diagram. A local licensed contractor handles installation. If that works for your project, this guide shows how to do it properly.

In Alpharetta, any signage over 4 square feet requires a permit, and the sign must meet the city's sign ordinance. The application asks for the business owner's details, the sign contractor's details, and an electrical permit for signs that use electricity. The city has up to 45 business days to approve or deny a complete application.
If you order factory-direct, plan the permit and the installer before production starts, not after the crate arrives.

blocks.text: Do You Need a Sign Permit in Alpharetta?

blocks.alt: Architectural elevation drawings and drafting tools for commercial sign permit submission

runs.text: Almost certainly yes for a channel letter sign. The City of Alpharetta's
sign permit page
says all signs must meet the established City Sign Ordinance and that any signage over 4 square feet requires a permit. A typical set of channel letters is far larger than that.
The rules sit in the city's Unified Development Code, in
Section 2.6, Signs
. Code sections change, so read the current version before you finalize your design, and confirm details with the city's Community Development staff.
The UDC lists what a sign permit application must contain. According to the code, that includes:

items.text: The business owner's name, address, telephone number, and business license number, along with the owner's signature authorizing placement of the sign
The sign contractor's name, address, telephone number, and business license number, along with the contractor's signature
An electrical permit, or a copy of one if it was already issued, for any sign that incorporates electricity

runs.text: In practice you will also need drawings that show the sign's size, location, materials, and mounting. Our
business sign permit guide
explains the typical packet, and the city's own forms and checklists are the final word.

The contractor requirement matters for factory-direct buyers. Because the application asks for contractor information, ask the city early whether an owner can install the sign or whether a licensed contractor must be named.
The UDC says applicants for signs that incorporate electricity must obtain an electrical permit or provide a copy of one. A lit channel letter sign falls in that category.
Electrical safety rules also apply. Under NEC Article 600, electric signs must be listed and installed according to their listing instructions, as this
EC&M overview of Article 600
explains. BASISSIGN lists UL 48 file number E555259 on its site. As with any manufacturer, you can verify a file number yourself in
UL Product iQ
. Our
UL 48 certification guide
explains what the listing covers.

blocks.text: How Long Does the City Take?

runs.text: The UDC sets an outer limit. A complete application must be approved or denied by the city's Director within 45 business days of receipt and payment of the required fees. The code also says that if the city fails to act within that period, the permit is deemed granted.

Two cautions apply. First, 45 business days is the legal limit, not a typical review time, so many applications move faster. Second, incomplete or non-conforming applications can be rejected, which restarts the clock. Do not install on a deemed approval without confirming your status with the city in writing.

title: Sign Permit Drawings: What Cities Actually Require (A Checklist With Real Examples)
excerpt: Picture a sign shop that submits a permit application with a polished mockup and a one-line description. The mockup looks great. The city rejects the submittal anyway. One county's published...
coverAlt: Sign Permit Drawings: What Cities Actually Require (A Checklist With Real Examples) — architectural commercial signage visual

blocks.alt: Sign permit drawings review with contractor on commercial building site

runs.text: Picture a sign shop that submits a permit application with a polished mockup and a one-line description. The mockup looks great. The city rejects the submittal anyway. One county's published checklist says it plainly: incomplete submittals will not be accepted.

That gap between a mockup and a permit drawing is where a lot of sign projects stall. A mockup is a sales picture. A permit drawing is a technical document that tells a plan reviewer where the sign goes, how big it is, how it is attached, and how it is powered.

This guide explains what a sign permit drawing set contains, using the published requirements of three real jurisdictions as examples. It is written for tenants, sign shops, agencies, and project managers who want the first submittal to be the last one.

Most cities want a site plan with the address, an elevation showing the sign's size and height, mounting and attachment details, electrical information for lit signs, a completed application, proof the property owner approves, and fees. Some also require engineer-stamped plans and a registered contractor.
Requirements vary by city, so find your jurisdiction's checklist before anything is drawn. The three examples below show how much they can differ.

blocks.alt: Commercial channel letter sign installation on building facade

rows.text: Show the client how the sign will look
Show the reviewer the sign is safe and compliant
Dimensions, heights, attachment, electrical, site context

runs.text: A good mockup helps you get landlord and client approval. It rarely satisfies a plan reviewer on its own.

blocks.text: What Three Real Jurisdictions Ask For

runs.text: These examples come from published city and county documents. They are not universal, and your city may ask for more or less.

rows.text: Site plan and vicinity map with the address, elevations and sections, and a sign permit application
Fees, contractor registration, a final inspection, and separate sub-permits if electrical work is needed. Published total of about 10 business days

A narrative, the address and parcel number, wet-stamped structural plans showing how the sign attaches to the wall, architectural plans with an elevation showing building height, sign height from grade, and sign dimensions, and wet-stamped electrical plans with the power source and a one-line riser where applicable
Fees, contractor licensing, inspections scheduled 48 hours ahead, and a rule that incomplete submittals are not accepted. Review is 10 business days at first and 5 for later rounds
A project narrative, a detailed site plan, construction drawings with dimensions, color elevations, elevations of existing signage, and mounting details where applicable
A landlord approval letter with printed name, title, date, and signature, plus a separate electrical permit if new wiring is needed. Published total of 20 business days

runs.text: The Maricopa guide is the oldest of the three, so check the city's current version before relying on it.

blocks.text: Anatomy of a Good Permit Drawing Set

runs.text: This shows where the building sits on the property and where the sign goes on the building. Include the address, and in some places the parcel number, as Adams County requires.

An elevation is a straight-on view of the building face with the sign drawn to scale. It should show the sign's overall dimensions, its height above grade, and its position on the wall. Color elevations are requested in some cities.

This is where many submittals fall short. A section drawing shows how the sign attaches, including the mounting method, anchors, and wall type. In Adams County, the structural plans must show how the sign is attached to the existing wall.
If you are still deciding between a raceway and flush letters, settle it before the drawings are made, because the mounting method changes the details.

Lit signs need electrical details. Adams County asks for the location of the power source and a one-line riser. Maricopa and Missouri City both note that new wiring can trigger a separate electrical permit or sub-permit.
Under NEC Article 600, electric signs must be listed and installed according to their listing instructions, as this
EC&M overview of Article 600
explains. Many cities also want the sign's listing information.
UL's signs page
describes the listing program.
List the materials, illumination type, colors, and letter heights. A reviewer should be able to confirm the sign matches what the code allows.
Maricopa also asks for plans or elevations showing existing signage with dimensions, since total sign area often counts everything already on the building.
A short written description of what is being installed. Both Adams County and Maricopa ask for one.
Plan reviewers are checking your sign against local rules, so the drawings need to show the numbers. Missouri City's bulletin gives a good sense of what those rules look like:

items.text: No more than two square feet of wall sign area for each linear foot of a business's frontage on a facade
An extra 33 percent of area for a lease space with walls facing two public streets
No wall sign within 100 feet of a residential property line
Channel letters and logos mounted flush, on a raceway, or on a wireway, with raceways painted to match the building
An unregistered logo limited to half of the sign area
Uniform materials, location, and illumination for signs in a shopping center

runs.text: Maricopa's guide describes a different formula for commercial zones, generally 1.5 square feet of sign area for every two linear feet of frontage with a 32 square foot maximum, and limits signs to 50 percent of the width of the wall.
The point is not to memorize these. It is that your drawing needs to show the sign area calculation, the frontage, and the setbacks clearly enough that the reviewer can check them in minutes.
Drawings are only part of the packet. Depending on the city, expect to provide:

items.text: A landlord or property owner approval letter. Maricopa specifies printed name, title, date, and signature.
Contractor registration or licensing. Missouri City and Adams County both require it before permits issue.
Engineer-stamped plans where required. Adams County asks for wet-stamped structural and electrical plans.
Fees. Adams County bases its plan review fee on a percentage of the listed valuation, so costs are not always flat.
Sign listing information for illuminated signs, which our
business sign permit guide
explains in more detail.

runs.text: Stamped documents come from licensed engineers, so ask early whether your city needs them and who will provide them.

Published timelines show why a complete first submittal matters. Adams County lists 10 business days for the first review and 5 for later reviews, and it charges an additional plan review fee for revisions after a permit is issued. Maricopa lists a total of 20 business days and 5 days for each review round.

Missouri City's bulletin breaks its roughly 10 business days into application processing, plan review, and comment processing, and notes that total time can increase if fees are paid late or extra reviews are needed.
Every resubmittal adds days. Every change after issuance can add days and cost.

blocks.alt: Commercial storefront building facade with illuminated exterior signage

runs.text: Some cities allow a temporary sign while the permanent one is in review. Missouri City allows a temporary wall sign after the permanent permit application is made, to be removed when the permanent sign is complete or 60 days after the application, whichever comes first. Maricopa limits banners to a 30-day temporary permit, issued only for situations such as a grand opening.
Check your city's rules before hanging anything.

title: Channel Letters vs Light Box Signs: The Complete Guide to Choosing the Right Sign for Your Business
excerpt: The rest of this guide explains every factor behind that advice, so you can make the decision with your eyes open instead of relying on a salesperson or a guess.
coverAlt: Channel Letters vs Light Box Signs: The Complete Guide to Choosing the Right Sign for Your Business — architectural commercial signage visual

blocks.alt: Channel Letters vs Light Box Signs: The Complete Guide to Choosing the Right Sign for Your Business

runs.text: If you only have thirty seconds, here is the summary.

items.text: Choose channel letters
when your sign is mainly a name or a logo, and you want a clean, modern, upscale look where the brand appears to float on the building.
Choose a light box
when your sign must carry more information, such as services, imagery or a changing message, or when you need a projecting sign that people see from the sidewalk.
Use both
when you want to win on two fronts: letters on the main facade for brand recognition, and a smaller light box projecting over the sidewalk for walk-up traffic.

runs.text: The rest of this guide explains every factor behind that advice, so you can make the decision with your eyes open instead of relying on a salesperson or a guess.

blocks.text: Why This Decision Is Harder Than It Looks

runs.text: Most business owners meet this question for the first time when they are opening or rebranding a location. They are busy with permits, staff, inventory and a hundred other things, and the sign feels like a box to tick.
But the sign is not a small decision. It is one of the few pieces of marketing that:

items.text: works every hour you are open, and every night you are closed,
is seen by every person who passes your location,
shapes the first impression before anyone walks in,
and stays in place for many years once it is installed.

runs.text: Channel letters and light boxes are the two most common illuminated sign types in the world. They can both look excellent and both be seen from far away at night. Yet they behave very differently on a building, in a budget and in daily use. Choosing the wrong one does not usually cause a disaster. It causes a slow mismatch between your sign and your business, and that is harder to notice and harder to fix.

Channel letters are individual three-dimensional letters or logo shapes. Each one is built as a hollow metal shell, typically aluminum, with a depth often measured in a few inches. Inside sits an LED lighting system, and the letter is finished with a face and a back.
The lighting style changes the way the letter behaves:

items.text: Front-lit:
the face is translucent acrylic, and light shines forward through it so the entire letter glows.
Halo-lit (back-lit):
the face is solid, and light shines backward onto the wall, creating a soft glow around the letter.
Front-and-back lit:
a combination of both, with a glowing face and a halo.
Non-illuminated metal letters:
polished, brushed or painted letters with no lighting at all, used for a refined daytime look.

runs.text: Because every letter is a separate piece, the wall remains visible between them. The building becomes part of the design, and the sign looks like it belongs to the architecture.

items.text: A brand name or logo that needs to be recognized quickly
Modern, upscale or design-led storefronts
Buildings with attractive brick, stone, glass or textured walls
Franchises that need consistent branding across many locations
Businesses that want a sign that reads clearly from the road
Messages with long lines of text, small details or photographs
Situations where the message changes often
Very intricate logos that have to be simplified to work as letters

runs.text: A light box is a sealed cabinet with a translucent face. LEDs inside light the entire panel, so the face glows evenly. The graphics are printed on, applied to, or built into the face.
There are several common variations:

items.text: Flat-face light boxes:
a simple glowing panel with printed or vinyl graphics.
Double-sided light boxes:
the same idea built to project from the wall so it can be seen from both directions along the sidewalk or street.
Embossed pan-face boxes:
the face is formed with raised shapes, so the letters or logo have dimension.
Push-through acrylic boxes:
the letters or logo are cut from thick acrylic and pushed through the face, so they rise out of the box and glow.
Projecting or blade signs seen by pedestrians
Menus, services lists and detailed graphics
Messages that need an easy way to update
Shopping-center pylon and plaza signs
Businesses that want a strong, simple, glowing presence at a modest build complexity
Facades where a rectangular box would fight the architecture
Premium brands that want the sign to feel integrated into the building
Walls with strong texture that make a flat box look pasted on

A single glowing panel with a defined rectangular shape
Detailed graphics, longer text, projecting signs
Excellent, since the whole face glows
A flat panel, with the style depending on the face

blocks.text: Twelve Questions That Decide the Right Choice

runs.text: Use these questions as a decision tool. Answer each one honestly, and note which sign style your answers point toward.

blocks.text: 1. What does the sign actually need to say?

runs.text: If the answer is a name, a logo and maybe a three-word descriptor, channel letters are usually the better fit. If the answer includes a list of services, a phone number or imagery, a light box carries the load more easily.
Drivers need short, large and bright. Pedestrians can handle more detail. Drivers point toward channel letters. Pedestrians point toward a projecting light box.

blocks.text: 3. How far away will people read it?

runs.text: A useful starting rule is one inch of letter height for every ten feet of viewing distance. Channel letters are very easy to size to a distance. Light boxes can hold large lettering too, but the box has to be proportioned to the wall.

blocks.text: 4. What does the building look like?

runs.text: A textured or architectural facade is usually flattered by channel letters. A plain, flat wall or a sign band can work well with either one. A light box on a beautiful brick wall may feel like an add-on, whereas letters feel like part of the building.
Modern, premium and design-led brands often favor channel letters. Friendly, practical and information-rich brands often favor light boxes. These are tendencies, not rules.

blocks.text: 6. How often will the message change?

runs.text: If you are a restaurant with changing specials, or a business that rebrands often, a light box face you can swap is practical. If your identity is stable, channel letters make a lasting statement.

blocks.text: 7. How much of your business happens after dark?

runs.text: Both sign types glow, but the way they glow differs. Front-lit channel letters give strong, crisp shapes. A light box gives a broad, even panel of light. For evening and roadside traffic, either works. Check the nighttime mockup for each.

blocks.text: 8. What do the landlord and city allow?

runs.text: Many shopping centers and cities set rules on the total sign area, the number of signs, the style of lighting and how far a sign can project. A projecting light box may need extra approval, because it extends over public space. Channel letters on a fascia are often more straightforward, though not always. Always check before you design.

blocks.text: 9. What does your budget look like over the whole life of the sign?

runs.text: Look beyond the first quote. Consider the build, the shipping, the installation, any permit costs and the long-term upkeep. The cheapest quote can be the most expensive sign if it fails early. Ask suppliers to quote both options so you can compare like for like.

blocks.text: 10. Do you need one sign or a system of signs?

runs.text: A lot of businesses need more than a single sign. A fascia sign for the road, a projecting sign for the sidewalk, and perhaps a door or window sign. In that case, designing them together gives a stronger, more consistent result.

blocks.text: 11. How will the sign be installed?

runs.text: Channel letters are mounted on the wall, usually with a template that positions every letter. A light box is mounted as a single unit and wired in one place. In both cases, a licensed electrician should handle the electrical connection. Ask your supplier what is provided in the box.

blocks.text: 12. Can you see the result before you commit?

runs.text: This may be the most important question. A mockup on a photo of your own building, in day and night views, answers more doubts than any article can.
These examples show how the decision plays out. They are starting points, not rules.
The neighborhood coffee shop on a busy corner.
The owner wants a warm, memorable look. Channel letters in a friendly brand color on the fascia handle the road, and a small double-sided light box over the sidewalk catches walkers.
The dental clinic in a professional building.
The brand needs to feel calm and trustworthy. Halo-lit channel letters on a clean wall create a quiet, premium look.
The pizza restaurant with a long menu.
Front-lit channel letters carry the name, while a light box near the entrance displays hours and specials that change.
The franchise rolling out twelve locations.
Consistency matters. Front-lit channel letters, built to one specification, make every location instantly recognizable.
The boutique hotel entrance.
The goal is elegance. Halo-lit or metal letters on stone, with no visible box, make the entrance feel integrated and high-end.
The service business in a strip plaza.
The shared pylon sign uses a light box panel, while the storefront has channel letters for the brand name.
The entertainment venue.
The sign should feel exciting. Front-and-back lit letters, with high-contrast halo depth, create a signature glow.

items.text: Choosing by looks in a design file alone.
A flat image cannot show how a sign sits on a real wall, in real light.
Putting too much text on channel letters.
Long lines shrink the letters and hurt readability.
Using a light box where the architecture wants letters.
The result can look like a sign stuck on a beautiful building.
Ignoring landlord and city rules until after the order.
Redesigns cost time and money.
Picking a thin script font for distance reading.
Fine details blur from far away.
Comparing quotes on price alone.
Certification, materials, LEDs, warranty and what is included all matter.
Forgetting about maintenance.
Ask who to call and what the warranty covers before you buy.

blocks.text: What to Check Before You Order Either Sign

runs.text: Whichever style you choose, the questions below separate a reliable supplier from a risky one.

items.text: Certification:
Is the sign UL certified for electrical safety? Ask for the file number so you can verify it independently.
Materials:
What type of aluminum, acrylic and finish is used, and how thick are they?
Lighting:
Which LED modules and power supplies are used, and how long are they rated to last?
Weather resistance:
Is the sign designed for rain, wind, heat and cold in your climate?
Warranty:
What does it cover, for how long, and what is the claim process?
What is in the box:
Is there a mounting template, a wiring diagram and the hardware you need?
Timeline:
What is the written production and shipping time from approval to delivery?
Mockup:
Can you see day and night views on your actual building before you pay?
Support:
Who do you contact if something goes wrong after installation?

runs.text: Both sign types should be installed by a qualified installer, and the electrical connection should be made by a licensed electrician. Before the day, confirm the power source location, the wall type and fixings, the mounting height, and any approvals you need. A one-to-one mounting template, as supplied with some orders, makes channel letter placement far more accurate, because every letter can be positioned against the real drilling pattern.
Modern LED signs need much less attention than older lighting, but they are not maintenance-free.

items.text: Clean the faces gently to remove dust and dirt, which can dim the glow.
Check periodically for loose fixings, damaged seals or moisture.
Keep a record of your order details and warranty terms.
If part of a sign goes dark, contact your supplier and electrician rather than opening it yourself.

blocks.text: How Channel Letters and Light Boxes Work Together

runs.text: The strongest storefront signage often combines both. A fascia sign made of channel letters tells the road who you are. A projecting light box tells the sidewalk what you offer. When they share colors, fonts and proportions, they read as one system and reinforce each other.
Plan the system together at the start. It is much easier to choose a consistent look in one design session than to match a new sign to an older one later.

items.question: Which is brighter, channel letters or a light box?

answerRuns.text: Both are very visible at night. A light box lights its whole face, so you see a broad area of light. Channel letters light only the letter shapes, which makes the name stand out crisply against the wall.

items.question: Which one is cheaper?

answerRuns.text: It depends on size, materials, design and installation. A simple light box can be less complex to build than a set of channel letters, but a large or double-sided box can cost more than a small set of letters. The only reliable way to compare is to request quotes for both.

items.question: Can I change the message later?

answerRuns.text: Often more easily with a light box, because the face can be replaced. Channel letters usually mean new or modified letters.

items.question: Are channel letters better for brand image?

answerRuns.text: Many owners feel they give a more premium, integrated look. That said, a well-designed light box can look excellent in the right setting.

items.question: Do I need a permit for either sign?

answerRuns.text: Often yes. Rules vary by city and property, and projecting signs may have additional requirements. Check with your landlord and local authority before ordering.

items.question: Can I use both types on one building?

answerRuns.text: Yes, and many businesses do. Just confirm the combined sign area stays within the local limits.

items.question: How long do these signs last?

answerRuns.text: Well-built aluminum and LED signs are designed for many years of outdoor use. The warranty and the quality of the components are the best clues, so ask for both in writing.

title: Front-Lit vs Halo-Lit Channel Letters: Which One Actually Brings in More Customers?
excerpt: The rest of this guide explains why, so you can choose with confidence instead of guessing.
coverAlt: Front-Lit vs Halo-Lit Channel Letters: Which One Actually Brings in More Customers? — architectural commercial signage visual

items.text: Choose front-lit letters
if you want maximum brightness and fast readability, especially on a busy road or a lively retail street.
Choose halo-lit (back-lit) letters
if you want a refined, premium look and your sign is read from closer range or in a design-led setting.
Choose front-and-back lit
if you want both: bright faces and a glowing halo.

runs.text: The rest of this guide explains why, so you can choose with confidence instead of guessing.
Your sign is often the first thing a customer experiences. The lighting style changes three things at once:

items.text: How far away people can read you at night.
What your brand feels like (energetic, upscale, modern, friendly).
How your sign looks in daylight, when most customers first notice it.

runs.text: Two signs with identical letters can feel completely different depending on how they are lit.
Front-lit letters are hollow metal letters with translucent acrylic faces. LED modules inside shine forward through the face, so the whole letter glows.
What it looks like:
Solid, bright, evenly lit letters. The color you choose for the acrylic is the color you see at night.

items.text: Very high visibility at night and from a distance
Bold, simple and easy to read at a glance
Works with almost any brand color
Familiar and trusted by customers, which suits retail and food
Less subtle than halo lighting, so it may feel too bright for ultra-luxury brands
Brand colors can look different when lit, so check the mockup at night

runs.text: Halo-lit letters have solid, opaque faces. LEDs sit inside and shine backward onto the wall, creating a glowing ring of light around each letter.
What it looks like:
Dark letters outlined by a soft glow, which gives the sign depth and a premium, almost floating look.

items.text: Elegant, upscale and modern
Looks great on stone, brick, concrete and textured walls
Less glare, with a calm and refined feel
The letters themselves can be metal, brushed finishes or colors that are visible in daylight
Less direct brightness, so it is harder to read from far away
Needs a suitable wall surface behind it, since the glow reflects off the wall
Needs enough standoff distance and the right wall color for the halo to show properly

runs.text: Also called combo or full-lit styles, these letters glow through the face and also cast a halo on the wall. They combine the readability of front-lit with the depth of halo-lit, and they make a strong statement at night.
They cost more to build than a single-lit style because there is more going on inside the letter, but many owners feel the presence is worth it for a flagship location.

rows.text: Typically the highest of the three

blocks.text: 3. What does your wall look like?

runs.text: Halo lighting needs a wall that can show the glow. A smooth, light or mid-tone surface helps the halo read well. Heavily textured, very dark or uneven walls may change the effect. A mockup on your real wall removes the guesswork.

blocks.text: 4. How much of your business happens at night?

runs.text: If evenings are your busiest hours, brightness is not a luxury. Front-lit or front-and-back lit will carry you farther.

blocks.text: 5. What do your landlord and city allow?

title: 9 Storefront Sign Mistakes That Quietly Cost You Customers (and How to Fix Each One)
excerpt: By BASISSIGN Editorial Team • 7 min read • Updated for Search

runs.text: Business Signage Guide • Retail Visibility
By
BASISSIGN Editorial Team
• 7 min read • Updated for Search
You have great products, fair prices and a team that cares. Yet people drive right past.

In many cases the problem is not your marketing. It is the sign above your door. A storefront sign is the only advertisement that works every hour you are open and every night you are closed, and it never sends an invoice. When it is wrong, it fails quietly. Nobody complains. They just keep driving.
The good news is that most sign problems are easy to spot once you know what to look for. Here are the nine we see most often, with a fix for each.

blocks.text: Mistake 1: Letters That Are Too Small to Read in Time

runs.text: What happens:
A driver needs a few seconds to notice, read and decide. If your letters are too small, those seconds run out before they reach your entrance.
The fix:
Start with the
1-inch-per-10-feet rule
. If customers first see your sign from 100 feet away, plan on letters about 10 inches tall or larger. Go up a size if you are on a faster road.
What happens:
A sign that lists your name, tagline, phone number, website and five services becomes a wall of text. People read none of it.
The fix:
Use your sign for one job:
be recognized
. Keep it to your business name and, at most, a short descriptor such as “Dental Care” or “Pizza”. Put the rest on your window, your website and your menu.

blocks.text: Mistake 3: Weak Contrast Between Letters and Background

runs.text: What happens:
Gray letters on a gray wall look classy in a design file. In real life, especially in afternoon glare, they vanish.
The fix:

Pair light letters with a dark background, or the reverse. Check your sign against the actual wall color in both daylight and at night. A mockup on a photo of your building makes this obvious before you spend anything.

blocks.text: Mistake 4: Choosing a Fancy Font Over a Readable One

runs.text: What happens:
Thin scripts and decorative fonts look beautiful on a business card. At 80 feet, the letters blur together.
The fix:

Choose clear, medium-to-bold letterforms for the sign, and keep the decorative font for the logo mark if it matters. Ask for a sign-ready version of your logo with simplified details. A good supplier will flag fonts that will not read well at distance.

blocks.text: Mistake 5: Choosing the Wrong Lighting Style

runs.text: What happens:
Each lighting style sends a different message and performs differently at night:

items.text: Front-lit letters:
Glow through the face. They are bright, bold and easy to read from far away.
Halo-lit letters:
Glow around the edge of a solid letter. They look refined and premium, but are subtler.
Front and back lit letters:
Combine both for maximum presence.
Non-illuminated metal letters:
Suit daytime-only businesses and architectural looks.

runs.text: Owners often pick halo-lit because it looks elegant, then discover it is too subtle for a busy roadside.
The fix:
Match the lighting to how your customers find you. If your business depends on evening or roadside traffic, brightness matters most.

blocks.text: Mistake 6: Ignoring the Landlord and City Until It Is Too Late

runs.text: What happens:

You approve a design and place the order. Then the landlord says the sign breaks the center’s criteria, or the city says it exceeds the allowed area. Now you are redesigning, waiting and possibly paying twice.
The fix:
Get the rules first:

items.text: Ask your landlord or property manager
for the written sign criteria.
Check your city’s sign ordinance
for maximum area, height and lighting rules.
Share those limits with your sign supplier
before the mockup.

title: How to Size Channel Letters: A Practical Guide to Letter Height, Viewing Distance and Readability
excerpt: A reliable starting point is 1 inch of letter height for every 10 feet of viewing distance. A customer reading your sign from 100 feet away needs letters about 10 inches tall. Traffic speed...
coverAlt: How to Size Channel Letters: A Practical Guide to Letter Height, Viewing Distance and Readability — architectural commercial signage visual

runs.text: A reliable starting point is 1 inch of letter height for every 10 feet of viewing distance. A customer reading your sign from 100 feet away needs letters about 10 inches tall. Traffic speed, building setback, letter style and local code can push that number up or down, and the rest of this guide shows you how.

blocks.text: Why Sign Size Is the Decision That Matters Most

runs.text: Owners spend weeks choosing colors and lighting styles, then pick a size by guessing. That is where most signs go wrong.

items.text: Too small:
drivers pass your entrance before they can read your name.
Too large:
the sign looks crowded, may break your city’s sign-area limit and can delay your permit.
Just right:
people read your name, recognize your brand and have time to turn in.

runs.text: Getting the size right before production costs nothing. Fixing it afterward means remaking the sign.

blocks.text: Step 1: Measure Your Real Viewing Distance

runs.text: Viewing distance is how far away your most important viewer will be when they first need to read the sign. It is not the distance from the door to the street.
Stand where a customer would first look for you, and measure from that spot to the sign. Common situations include:

items.text: Walk-up retail in a plaza: 30 to 60 feet.
Strip-mall storefront with a parking lot: 60 to 150 feet.
Roadside business with a setback: 150 feet or more.

runs.text: If you have more than one angle, such as a street and a parking lot, size for the longer one.

blocks.text: Step 2: Use the Letter Height Rule of Thumb

runs.text: The table below applies the 1-inch-per-10-feet guideline. Treat it as the minimum for comfortable reading, not a maximum.
Signs that are read at a glance work best at the larger end. A lobby sign that people study while waiting can sit at the smaller end.
A driver at 35 mph covers roughly 51 feet every second. At 45 mph it is about 66 feet per second. That leaves very little time to notice, read and react.

items.text: Under 30 mph:
the base rule is usually enough.
30 to 45 mph:
go one size up, or keep the message short.
Above 45 mph:
use the largest letters your frontage and code allow, and keep the text to the business name only.

runs.text: Short messages beat big messages. Three words at 12 inches are easier to read at speed than six words at 8 inches.

blocks.text: Step 4: Check Your Font and Stroke Width

runs.text: Two signs with the same letter height can read very differently.

items.text: Simple sans-serif fonts read faster from a distance than thin script or decorative fonts.
Thicker strokes hold up better at night because the lit area is larger.
Tight spacing makes letters merge. Wider letter spacing helps, especially for halo-lit letters.
Thin script logos often need to be scaled up or simplified for signage. This is normal, and a good manufacturer will tell you before production.

runs.text: If your logo has very fine details, ask for a simplified sign version that keeps the brand look while staying legible.

blocks.text: Step 5: Match the Size to Your Lighting Style

runs.text: The way a letter is lit changes how large it needs to look.

rows.text: Best for reading at distance and for most storefronts
Looks refined, but is subtler, so go a little larger for roadside use
Depends on daylight and contrast, so size up for dark backgrounds

runs.text: Contrast matters as much as size. White letters on a dark wall will read farther than dark letters on a mid-tone wall at the same height.

blocks.text: Step 6: Fit the Sign to the Wall

runs.text: A sign should look like it belongs to the building.

items.text: Leave breathing room.
Many designers keep a margin of roughly 20 to 25 percent of the sign’s height above and below the letters.
Cover about 50 to 70 percent
of the available sign band as a starting point. Edge-to-edge looks cramped.
Center on architectural features
such as doors, windows or the storefront’s sign band, so the sign lines up with the building.
Mind obstacles
like lights, vents, awnings and roof edges.

blocks.text: Step 7: Check Local Sign Rules Before You Order

runs.text: Cities and landlords often limit the total sign area, the number of signs and the letter height. Many codes tie the allowed area to the width of your storefront, and landlords of shopping centers frequently add their own criteria on top.
Before you approve a design:

items.text: Ask your landlord or property manager for their sign criteria.
Check your city’s sign ordinance or call the planning department.
Confirm the maximum area and any rules on lighting.
Share those limits with your sign supplier so the mockup respects them.

runs.text: BASISSIGN’s
business sign permit guide
walks through the approval process in more detail.
A café owner has a storefront facing a parking lot, with customers first noticing the sign from about 80 feet away.

items.text: Base height:
80 ft ÷ 10 = 8 in. Because the sign must catch the eye of people arriving by car, she steps up to 10 to 12 in.
Lighting:
front-lit letters for the strongest night reading.
Layout:
a two-word name on one line, with about a quarter of the sign height as clear space above and below.
Check:
the total sign area stays within the landlord’s limit.

runs.text: The result is a sign that reads clearly from the parking lot without overpowering the facade.

items.text: Choosing a size from a screen mockup without checking it against the real wall.
Adding a tagline that forces the main name to shrink.
Ignoring the viewing angle from the road.
Forgetting that dark letters on a dark wall lose size visually.
Ordering before confirming the landlord’s maximum.

answerRuns.text: It depends on speed and setback, but many roadside businesses need 18 to 24 inches or more. Use the rule above and confirm with local code.

title: UL 48, UL 879, UL 8750, and UL 1310: Which UL Standard Applies to Your LED Sign?
excerpt: Picture an electrician unpacking a crate of channel letters on install day. The sign label says UL 48. The power supply label says UL 8750 and UL 1310. A third label on the LED modules...
coverAlt: UL 48, UL 879, UL 8750, and UL 1310: Which UL Standard Applies to Your LED Sign? — architectural commercial signage visual

runs.text: Picture an electrician unpacking a crate of channel letters on install day. The sign label says UL 48. The power supply label says UL 8750 and UL 1310. A third label on the LED modules mentions something else. The inspector walks up and asks which standard the sign was actually evaluated under.

It is a fair question, and it trips up experienced people. UL publishes several standards that touch an LED sign, and they are not interchangeable. Quote the wrong one on a permit form, or assume a listed power supply makes the whole sign listed, and you can lose a week to a failed inspection.

This guide explains what UL 48, UL 879, UL 8750, and UL 1310 each cover, how they fit together, and how to read the labels on a sign. It is written for sign shops, electricians, project managers, and anyone who has to answer the inspector’s question.

UL 48 is the standard for the complete electric sign. UL 879 covers the components made for use in signs. UL 8750 covers LED equipment, and UL 1310 covers Class 2 power units. They work together as layers, not as competitors.
What an inspector cares about most is simple. Is the sign listed, and is it installed according to its listing? That requirement comes from the National Electrical Code.

blocks.text: UL 48: The Standard for Electric Signs

runs.text: UL 48 is the standard for the finished electric sign. It is a product-level standard, so it evaluates the sign as a whole, including its construction, wiring, enclosure, and electrical parts. The federal OSHA list of standards for which nationally recognized testing laboratories are approved includes
UL 48, Electric Signs
It connects directly to code. Under NEC Article 600, electric signs and outline lighting must be listed and installed according to their listing instructions, as this
EC&M overview of Article 600
explains.
UL’s signs page
describes the sign program.
LED signs are not a special exception. UL 48 includes supplementary requirements for signs that use Class 2 LED illumination systems, covering things like how Class 2 circuits must be wired, as an
Intertek standards update notice for UL 48
summarizes.
UL 879 is the standard for components made for use in signs. UL Standards and Engagement’s
summary of UL 879
describes it as covering components for signs and outline lighting systems intended for installation under the NEC.
In practice, that includes electronic equipment for signs such as LED units and LED power sources, as this
Signs of the Times article on UL 879
explains. A related standard, UL 879A, covers LED sign and sign retrofit kits, according to an accreditation scope that lists it.
Think of UL 879 as the component layer. A component that meets it is built to go inside a sign. It is not a sign by itself.
UL 8750 is the safety standard for light emitting diode equipment used in lighting products. It covers LED modules, drivers, and related parts.
The important point is how it relates to UL 48. UL’s own
guidance for code authorities on LED signs and luminaires

explains that the end product is evaluated under its own standard, such as UL 48 for electric signs or UL 1598 for luminaires, and that the LED requirements in UL 8750 supplement those basic product requirements. In short, UL 8750 helps make an LED sign compliant, but it does not replace UL 48.

UL 1310 covers Class 2 power units, which are power supplies designed with limited output energy to reduce the risk of electric shock and fire. Many LED signs use a Class 2, low-voltage secondary circuit, which is why you see UL 1310 on power supply labels. OSHA’s list also includes
UL 1310, Class 2 Power Units
A Class 2 supply on its own does not make the complete sign listed. It is one component inside the sign, and the sign still has to be evaluated as a whole.

A useful way to picture it is a chain. The complete sign is evaluated to UL 48. Inside it, the LED modules and drivers meet UL 8750 and the sign component standard UL 879, and the Class 2 power supply meets UL 1310.

blocks.text: Listed vs Recognized: Reading the Labels

runs.text: In the UL system, complete products can be Listed, while components intended for use inside other products are generally Recognized. A recognized component is not the same as a listed sign.

So the label that matters most for an inspector is the one on the finished sign. A listed power supply inside an unlisted sign does not make the sign compliant, and a listed sign should carry its own label and file information.
When you unbox a sign, check three things:

items.text: That the sign itself carries a listing label
That the label shows a file number or other identifying information
That the components inside match the documentation you were given

blocks.text: What Inspectors and Property Managers Look For

runs.text: Inspectors look for a listed sign installed according to its listing instructions, with the label visible and the mounting secure. Property managers and landlords often ask for the same proof before approving an installation.
Having the documentation ready saves time. Our
business sign permit guide
explains the drawings and paperwork most cities ask for, and our
UL 48 certification guide
covers why the listing matters.
Do not rely on a claim alone. Ask the supplier for the UL file number, then search it in
UL Product iQ
. UL also maintains a
sign components database
for the component layer.
Confirm the company name and product category match what you are buying, and check that the label on the delivered sign matches the file.

blocks.text: Which Standard Applies to Which Sign Type

rows.text: Our product page states UL 48 listing and NEC Article 600 construction
Our product page states UL 48 listing and pre-wiring to NEC Article 600

runs.text: UL 48 applies to electric signs. Signs with no electrical components, such as non-illuminated architectural facade elements, do not have an electrical UL 48 listing requirement, though structural mounting rules still apply.

items.text: Is the complete sign listed to UL 48, and what is the file number?
Which standards do the LED modules and power supply meet, such as UL 8750, UL 879, and UL 1310?
Is the power supply Class 2, and what is its output rating?
Where on the sign is the listing label?
What documentation comes with the order for the permit?
Does the listing cover the exact configuration I am ordering?

runs.text: Our
warranty policy
also matters here, since unauthorized electrical changes can affect both coverage and the listing.

runs.text: Picture an experiential marketing agency installing a brand name in six-foot marquee letters at a convention center. The letters look great in the warehouse. The night before load-in, venue electrical staff ask for proof that the lit signage is UL listed. Nobody has the paperwork, and the sign sits in a crate while the booth opens without it.

Marquee letters are one of the easiest signs to fall in love with and one of the easiest to buy badly. The look is simple, but the details that decide whether a set survives a rental season, passes a venue check, or holds up on a wall are not obvious from a photo.

This guide covers what marquee channel letters are, how the types and sizes differ, how bulbs and power work, what UL 48 means for these signs, and what wholesale buyers should ask before ordering a full set.

Marquee channel letters are open-face letters lined with exposed LED bulbs, built either to stand on a base plate or to mount on a wall. For events and trade shows, buy UL-listed letters, because many venues require UL-listed electrical equipment. For rental businesses and agencies, focus on frame durability, replaceable bulbs, packing, and written documentation as much as price.

Marquee channel letters have no acrylic face. Instead, individual bulbs sit around the letter outline, giving the vintage theater-marquee look. Standard channel letters work the other way, with an enclosed face that diffuses light evenly.
Modern versions use LED bulbs instead of the hot, fragile incandescent bulbs of old marquees. Our

title: How Long Does a Business Sign Take? A Realistic Timeline From Design to Final Inspection
excerpt: Picture a restaurant group with a fixed opening date. The signs are ordered six weeks out, which feels generous. Then the landlord’s approval letter takes two weeks, the city permit takes...
coverAlt: How Long Does a Business Sign Take? A Realistic Timeline From Design to Final Inspection — architectural commercial signage visual

runs.text: Picture a restaurant group with a fixed opening date. The signs are ordered six weeks out, which feels generous. Then the landlord’s approval letter takes two weeks, the city permit takes three, and the crate ships a week later than planned. Opening day arrives with a vinyl banner where the channel letters should be.

None of those delays were unusual. Each one was predictable, and each one was easy to plan around. The mistake was treating a sign as a single production task when it is really seven steps, and only one of them happens in the factory.

This guide breaks down the full timeline of a business sign project, from the first mockup to the final inspection. It uses published permit review times from city and county governments, plus the production windows on our own product pages, so you can build a schedule that holds.

A simple sign in a city with fast permitting can be done in 3 to 5 weeks. A typical commercial project, with landlord approval and a standard permit review, runs 7 to 11 weeks when the steps happen one after another. Historic districts, variances, and multi-site rollouts can stretch to 3 to 5 months.
The factory is rarely the bottleneck. Approvals are.

blocks.text: The Seven Phases at a Glance

rows.text: A few days to several weeks

This phase is entirely in your hands. You supply the logo, the size, the location, and the lighting style, and the manufacturer returns a mockup. Our process offers a free mockup, usually within 24 hours of a complete submission.
The delay here is almost always on the client side. Waiting on brand approvals, changing the logo version, or revising colors can add days or weeks before anything is built.

Send vector artwork, a photo of the wall with something in frame for scale, and the landlord’s sign criteria if you have them. A complete brief shortens this phase more than anything else. For sizing help, see our guidance on how viewing distance affects letter height.

If you lease the space, your landlord almost certainly has a say. Many leases limit sign size, color, lighting, and mounting method, and many cities will not accept a permit application without a letter of authorization from the property owner.

This step has the widest range of any phase. A small owner may approve in a day. A property management company with a design review committee can take weeks. Start it the moment your mockup is ready, and run it alongside permit preparation, not after it.
Our

Most cities require a permit for a permanent exterior sign, and review times vary more than people expect. Here is what a handful of US city and county governments publish about their own timelines.

Two details from these pages matter for scheduling. First, some jurisdictions state that incomplete applications need more review time, and Adams County’s shorter second-review window rewards getting the first submittal right. Second, Maricopa notes that a separate electrical permit is required when a wall sign needs new wiring, so ask your city whether one applies.

The fix is simple. Submit complete shop drawings the first time, with elevation views, mounting details, and electrical information. We provide permit-ready drawings and UL documentation with orders, and our
UL 48 certification guide

Those windows start when the design is final. Changes after production begins can affect both timing and cost, so lock the artwork, size, and colors before you approve.

Some project teams start fabrication while the permit is still in review to save time. That can work, but it carries risk, because a reviewer’s comment can force a change after the sign is built. Decide that tradeoff deliberately, and never install before the permit is approved.
Shipping time depends on distance, carrier, and sign size. Larger signs often ship by freight on pallets or in crates, which adds scheduling steps, such as delivery appointments and liftgate service.

Plan to be on site when it arrives. Inspect the crate for damage before the driver leaves, and report any issues right away.

As a planning figure, a straightforward single-story storefront sign takes a small crew about 4 to 6 hours to mount, and a licensed electrician typically needs another hour or two for the final connection. Larger signs, masonry walls, and raceway systems take longer. Our

The delay risk here is scheduling. Electricians and lift rental can be booked days or weeks out, so reserve them while the permit is in review, not after the sign arrives.

Many permits require a final inspection after installation. Inspectors commonly check that the sign is securely mounted and that its listing label is visible. Booking the inspection can take a few days, and a failed inspection adds another round.
Bring your permit, your sign’s listing information, and the installer’s contact details. Fixing a loose mount or a missing label on the spot is far cheaper than a second visit.

blocks.text: Seven Ways to Shorten the Timeline

runs.text: The biggest wins come from the steps that are not in the factory.

Start landlord approval and permit preparation at the same time as the mockup. Submit complete shop drawings on the first try, since resubmittals add review rounds. Ask your city whether an electrical permit is separate and file both together if so. Book the electrician and the inspection while the permit is under review. For multi-site rollouts, standardize the sign spec after the first store so later orders skip the design phase. Our

The most common cause is starting too late, often after the lease is signed and the opening date is already set.
The second is unclear landlord criteria. If nobody has confirmed size, mounting, or color rules, the design gets reworked mid-project.
The third is incomplete permit drawings. A reviewer’s request for more detail adds a full review round.
The fourth is late design changes. Revisions after production starts affect both the schedule and the budget.
The fifth is installation scheduling. The sign arrives, and the electrician is booked for next week.
The last is skipping the buffer. Plans that leave zero slack turn small delays into missed openings.

title: How Long Does a Business Sign Take? A Realistic Timeline From Design to Final Inspection
excerpt: Picture a restaurant group with a fixed opening date. The signs are ordered six weeks out, which feels generous. Then the landlord’s approval letter takes two weeks, the city permit takes...
coverAlt: How Long Does a Business Sign Take? A Realistic Timeline From Design to Final Inspection — architectural commercial signage visual

runs.text: Picture a restaurant group with a fixed opening date. The signs are ordered six weeks out, which feels generous. Then the landlord’s approval letter takes two weeks, the city permit takes three, and the crate ships a week later than planned. Opening day arrives with a vinyl banner where the channel letters should be.

None of those delays were unusual. Each one was predictable, and each one was easy to plan around. The mistake was treating a sign as a single production task when it is really seven steps, and only one of them happens in the factory.

This guide breaks down the full timeline of a business sign project, from the first mockup to the final inspection. It uses published permit review times from city and county governments, plus the production windows on our own product pages, so you can build a schedule that holds.

A simple sign in a city with fast permitting can be done in 3 to 5 weeks. A typical commercial project, with landlord approval and a standard permit review, runs 7 to 11 weeks when the steps happen one after another. Historic districts, variances, and multi-site rollouts can stretch to 3 to 5 months.
The factory is rarely the bottleneck. Approvals are.

rows.text: A few days to several weeks
About 3 working days to 30 days, longer for special districts
About 4 to 8 working days for channel letters, 10 to 12 days for blade cabinets
About 1 week, varies by distance and method
Half a day to a day, plus electrician

This phase is entirely in your hands. You supply the logo, the size, the location, and the lighting style, and the manufacturer returns a mockup. Our process offers a free mockup, usually within 24 hours of a complete submission.
The delay here is almost always on the client side. Waiting on brand approvals, changing the logo version, or revising colors can add days or weeks before anything is built.

Send vector artwork, a photo of the wall with something in frame for scale, and the landlord’s sign criteria if you have them. A complete brief shortens this phase more than anything else. For sizing help, see our guidance on how viewing distance affects letter height.

This step has the widest range of any phase. A small owner may approve in a day. A property management company with a design review committee can take weeks. Start it the moment your mockup is ready, and run it alongside permit preparation, not after it.

About two weeks, and sign permit applications may not be expedited

Second, Maricopa notes that a separate electrical permit is required when a wall sign needs new wiring, so ask your city whether one applies.

The fix is simple. Submit complete shop drawings the first time, with elevation views, mounting details, and electrical information. We provide permit-ready drawings and UL documentation with orders, and our

This is the part people picture, and it is often the shortest. Our

and

Those windows start when the design is final. Changes after production begins can affect both timing and cost, so lock the artwork, size, and colors before you approve.

Some project teams start fabrication while the permit is still in review to save time. That can work, but it carries risk, because a reviewer’s comment can force a change after the sign is built. Decide that tradeoff deliberately, and never install before the permit is approved.
Shipping time depends on distance, carrier, and sign size. Larger signs often ship by freight on pallets or in crates, which adds scheduling steps, such as delivery appointments and liftgate service.

In the scenarios below, we assume about a week for shipping. Treat that as a planning figure and ask your supplier for a delivery date on your actual order. Also confirm how the sign is packed, since reinforced crating protects letters in transit.
Plan to be on site when it arrives. Inspect the crate for damage before the driver leaves, and report any issues right away.

As a planning figure, a straightforward single-story storefront sign takes a small crew about 4 to 6 hours to mount, and a licensed electrician typically needs another hour or two for the final connection. Larger signs, masonry walls, and raceway systems take longer. Our

The delay risk here is scheduling. Electricians and lift rental can be booked days or weeks out, so reserve them while the permit is in review, not after the sign arrives.

Many permits require a final inspection after installation. Inspectors commonly check that the sign is securely mounted and that its listing label is visible. Booking the inspection can take a few days, and a failed inspection adds another round.
Bring your permit, your sign’s listing information, and the installer’s contact details. Fixing a loose mount or a missing label on the spot is far cheaper than a second visit.

If that date has already passed, you need either rush production where available, parallel work, or a temporary sign for opening day. Knowing early is worth more than any single step you can speed up.

runs.text: The biggest wins come from the steps that are not in the factory.

Start landlord approval and permit preparation at the same time as the mockup. Submit complete shop drawings on the first try, since resubmittals add review rounds. Ask your city whether an electrical permit is separate and file both together if so. Book the electrician and the inspection while the permit is under review. For multi-site rollouts, standardize the sign spec after the first store so later orders skip the design phase. Our

The second is unclear landlord criteria. If nobody has confirmed size, mounting, or color rules, the design gets reworked mid-project.
The third is incomplete permit drawings. A reviewer’s request for more detail adds a full review round.
The fourth is late design changes. Revisions after production starts affect both the schedule and the budget.
The fifth is installation scheduling. The sign arrives, and the electrician is booked for next week.
The last is skipping the buffer. Plans that leave zero slack turn small delays into missed openings.

title: Stainless Steel vs Aluminum Channel Letters: Which Metal Should You Specify?
excerpt: Picture two quotes on the same desk this week. One is a seaside resort that wants brushed metal letters over the entrance. The other is a suburban office park with forty identical tenant...
coverAlt: Stainless Steel vs Aluminum Channel Letters: Which Metal Should You Specify? — architectural commercial signage visual

runs.text: Picture two quotes on the same desk this week. One is a seaside resort that wants brushed metal letters over the entrance. The other is a suburban office park with forty identical tenant signs. Same product category, completely different metal decisions.

Aluminum or stainless steel sounds like a simple question until you ask what the sign will look like in five years, how it handles salt air, and whether the wall can carry the weight. Pick well and the sign looks sharp for a decade. Pick badly and you get brown streaks, chalky paint, or a surprise bill for stronger anchors.

This guide compares the two metals the way a specifier needs them compared: corrosion, weight, finish, cost, and care. It also covers the grade question that trips up coastal projects, 304 versus 316 stainless, and the hardware detail that quietly ruins mixed-metal signs.

Aluminum is the default for most channel letters. It is light, resists corrosion on its own, forms and paints easily, and costs less. For storefronts, rollouts, and large letters, it is usually the practical choice.

Stainless steel is the premium option. Choose it when you want a true brushed or mirror metal look, extra resistance to dents, or an upscale architectural finish. For coastal sites, pools, and areas with heavy road salt, specify 316 grade, not 304, and plan on regular cleaning.

blocks.text: How Each Metal Is Used in Channel Letters

runs.text: A channel letter has a few metal parts. The return is the side wall that gives the letter its depth. The back closes the letter at the wall. On front-lit letters the face is acrylic, while on halo-lit and non-illuminated letters the face itself can be metal.
BASISSIGN’s
front-lit channel letters
use aluminum returns with an acrylic face. Our
back-lit halo letters
are built from stainless steel in 304 or 316 grade, or from aluminum, in thicknesses of roughly 0.040 to 0.063 inch. Our
perforated return and open face letters
use heavy-gauge aluminum or stainless steel returns.

Aluminum protects itself. When it meets air, it forms a thin, hard oxide film that shields the metal underneath, and the film re-forms if it gets scratched. Paint, powder coating, or anodizing adds more protection and gives you the color you need. You can read more about the metal on
The Aluminum Association’s site
It also weighs about one-third as much as steel, which makes large letters easier to handle, ship, and mount. It cuts, bends, and welds readily, which keeps fabrication time and cost down.

Stainless steel resists corrosion because of its chromium content, which forms a passive surface layer. The two grades you will see most are 304 and 316. Grade 304 is the general-purpose workhorse. Grade 316 adds molybdenum, which improves resistance to pitting from chlorides such as salt air, pool chemicals, and road salt.

Stainless is harder than aluminum, so it resists dents and scratches better, and it gives a metal finish that paint cannot fully imitate. It is also heavier, tougher to cut and form, and usually more expensive.

blocks.text: Stainless Steel vs Aluminum: Side by Side

rows.text: About one-third the weight of steel
Roughly three times heavier than aluminum
Natural oxide film, plus paint or anodizing
Passive chromium layer, with 316 for coastal and salt exposure
Painted or powder-coated in any color, anodized, brushed
Brushed, polished, mirror, and custom painted
Easy to cut, bend, and weld
Tougher to cut and form, more labor
Wipe clean, touch up chipped paint
Keep clean, watch for fingerprints and salt deposits
Storefronts, rollouts, large letters, budget-sensitive jobs
Lobbies, luxury brands, architectural facades, coastal sites (316)

runs.text: Both metals resist corrosion, but neither is immune. The details decide which one fits your site.

Aluminum rarely rusts, but if its paint or anodized finish is damaged in salty air, the exposed metal can develop a white, chalky oxidation. That is mostly cosmetic, and it is why the coating system matters as much as the metal.
Stainless steel can be attacked by chlorides, which break down its protective layer. The Nickel Institute’s guide to
stainless steel in exterior architecture
stresses choosing the right grade for the site, and notes that marine salts can travel much further inland than people expect.
One industry body, the South African Stainless Steel Development Association, recommends
316 or better for exterior use within about 4 kilometers of the sea
, with 304 acceptable inland. The British Stainless Steel Association goes further in its
care guidance
, listing 304 as not recommended in coastal or marine locations and suggesting cleaning 316 every 6 to 12 months there.

Even 316 is not maintenance free. In coastal or humid air, stainless can develop brown surface discoloration known as tea staining. It looks like rust but is usually cosmetic, and regular cleaning removes it.
Smoother finishes help. A technical datasheet from
Aalco on stainless steel in coastal environments
names grade 316 with a mirror polished finish as the best choice for long life and good appearance, because contaminants cling less to a smooth surface.

blocks.text: Coastal, Pool, and Winter Salt Locations

runs.text: Use this as a starting point, then confirm with your manufacturer.

In an inland, dry climate, painted aluminum or 304 stainless both work well. Near the coast, around pools or spas, or where roads are heavily salted, choose 316 stainless or a well-coated aluminum, and build a cleaning routine into your maintenance plan.
If a project sits in between, such as a few miles from the sea, ask the manufacturer what they have seen perform in your area. Local experience is worth more than a general rule.

Stainless steel letters weigh roughly three times as much as aluminum letters of the same size. On small letters that hardly matters. On large letters, long raceways, or thin facades, it changes the anchor plan.
Weight also affects shipping cost and the crew you need on install day. Send your wall details and letter sizes with your quote request so the mounting hardware is matched to the metal. Our
installation resources
explain the common mounting methods.
Aluminum is the color specialist. It can be painted or powder-coated to match a brand color closely, which is why it suits rollouts where every location must look the same.

Stainless steel is the metal specialist. Brushed finishes hide minor scratches and give a refined, directional grain. Polished and mirror finishes look dramatic but show fingerprints and water spots, so they suit locations people cannot touch. BASISSIGN also offers custom painted finishes on stainless when the design calls for it.
Upfront, aluminum usually costs less, and 316 stainless costs more than 304. That is only part of the picture.

Painted aluminum can need touch-ups over time, and stainless needs periodic cleaning in harsh air. For a flagship location where the look is the brand, the premium for stainless can be easy to justify. For a forty-location rollout, painted aluminum often delivers the consistency and budget you need. Our
channel letter cost guide
covers what drives the overall price.

blocks.text: Mixing Metals: The Galvanic Corrosion Trap

runs.text: This is the detail that quietly ruins good signs. When two different metals touch in a wet or salty environment, the less noble one can corrode faster. Stainless steel fasteners against an aluminum letter are a classic example.
The Nickel Institute’s
maintenance and cleaning guidelines
point to electrically insulating stainless steel from dissimilar components as a way to avoid this. In practice, that means isolating washers or sleeves, compatible hardware, and a clean install.
The opposite problem matters too. Plain carbon steel hardware or tools can leave iron particles that rust and stain a stainless face. Ask your manufacturer how hardware is chosen and isolated.

blocks.text: Which Metal for Which Letter Style

rows.text: Stainless is popular for upscale and corporate looks
Perforated return and open face letters
Lower cost, easy color matching, light to mount
Salt air demands the right grade and a cleaning plan
Premium look, and 304 is usually fine inside

runs.text: See how this plays out in our
hospitality signage projects
and
corporate and professional signage
Two quotes can look identical and still use different metal. These questions keep you comparing like with like:

items.text: Which alloy and grade is used, 304 or 316 for stainless, and what thickness?
How are aluminum parts finished, painted, powder-coated, or anodized?
How is hardware chosen and isolated to prevent galvanic corrosion?
What does each letter weigh, and what mounting load should I plan for?
Can I see a finish sample before approving production?
What does the warranty cover on the structure? BASISSIGN lists 5 years on structure, detailed on our
warranty policy page
What cleaning routine do you recommend for my location?

runs.text: For aluminum, wipe with mild soap, water, and a soft cloth, and touch up chipped paint before moisture gets underneath.

For stainless steel, clean along the grain with a soft, non-abrasive cloth. Aalco warns against cloths contaminated with iron or mild steel, and against cleaning products that damage the polished surface. In coastal areas, rinse with fresh water now and then, and follow the cleaning interval your manufacturer or the BSSA guidance suggests.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes When Choosing a Metal

runs.text: The most common mistake is specifying 304 stainless for a coastal site to save money. It may look fine at handover and stain within a season.
The second is assuming stainless never needs cleaning. Even 316 needs regular care in salty or humid air.
The third is mixing metals without isolating the hardware, which can corrode the softer metal around every fastener.
The fourth is ignoring weight. Large stainless letters can change the anchor plan, and that is better discovered before ordering than on install day.
The last is comparing quotes without comparing alloys and thicknesses. A cheaper quote may simply be thinner metal or a lower grade.

items.question: Is stainless steel better than aluminum for channel letters?

answerRuns.text: Not always. Stainless steel gives a premium metal look and resists dents, while aluminum is lighter, easier to color match, and costs less. For most storefronts, aluminum is the practical choice, and stainless is the upgrade for upscale or coastal projects.

items.question: Do I need 316 stainless steel for outdoor channel letters?

answerRuns.text: If the sign is near the coast, a pool, or heavily salted roads, 316 is the safer choice. Inland and away from salt, 304 is generally acceptable. Always confirm with your manufacturer for your specific location.

items.question: Does aluminum rust?

answerRuns.text: Aluminum does not rust the way iron does. It forms a protective oxide film, but damaged paint or anodizing in salty air can lead to white, chalky oxidation, so keep the finish intact.

items.question: Why does stainless steel get brown stains outdoors?

answerRuns.text: That is usually tea staining, a surface discoloration caused by salt, humidity, or iron contamination. It is typically cosmetic and comes off with proper cleaning, but it is more likely with lower grades and rough finishes.

items.question: Which metal is cheaper for channel letters?

answerRuns.text: Aluminum is usually cheaper upfront. Stainless costs more, and 316 costs more than 304. Compare total cost over time, including finish upkeep and cleaning.

runs.text: The resort and the office park from the start of this guide do not need the same metal, and that is the point. Match the metal to the environment, the wall, and the brand, not to habit.
